Source code has all of these features today; one CDK redeploy of ig-dev-services rebuilds the asset and closes specialist routing + RBAC + EventBridge in a single change (F-1, the load-bearing follow-up). Built (PR #733, CI 32/32 green, NOT yet merged/deployed — merge awaiting approval): push_to_user() walked _user_sessions, an in-memory dict of native FastAPI sockets held by the ECS task. No frontend change — useMeridianJob already settles on a job_complete frame and cancels the poll; the client had been waiting for a frame that never came.

Verified: 17 new tests pass and 3 fail against the pre-fix baseline (source stashed and re-run), so they catch the bug rather than pass by construction; related suites 26 failed/187 passed vs 26 failed/170 passed baseline with byte-identical failure sets (zero new); cdk diff shows the GSI is an in-place update, not a table replacement; and identity alignment was checked against live data (ws-proxy stores the Cognito sub, chat_async uses claims["sub"], live staging-b rows carry real subs) because a mismatch would have made the fix silently do nothing.

MERGED 31420574 (CI 6/6, MERGEABLE/CLEAN). agent-engine-stack.ts now declares desiredCount 1 for staging-b; takes effect on the next staging-b deploy. Docker-bundled synth verified: stg-b 1, dev 0 unchanged.

CORRECTION — the drop does NOT self-heal. I had written that autoscaling (MinCapacity=1) restored the service and my manual scale-up was redundant. CloudTrail says otherwise: every UpdateService call in both windows was either cloudformation.amazonaws.com setting 0, or a human on a laptop setting 1 — zero application-autoscaling callers. stg-b: CFN→0 at 13:45:01Z, manual→1 at 13:51:07Z. dev: CFN→0 at 03:23:12Z, manual→1 at 03:29:21Z.

Why the metric misled: DesiredTaskCount shows the gap closing on its own and reads exactly like self-healing — it shows recovery happened, not who did it. A MinCapacity=1 target can’t rescue this regardless: target-tracking reacts to utilization alarms and a service at 0 tasks emits none. Severity is higher, not lower — a hard outage until someone notices. The earlier “don’t manual-scale” guidance is withdrawn.

Still exposed: dev deliberately left at 0 in #738 (bootstrap case needs its own call) — it 503’d from exactly this on 2026-07-31 during #733’s deploy. #737 (another terminal) fixed a separate contributor: the CI roll job restoring dev’s autoscaling floor to a hardcoded 0.

Method note: three successive diagnoses of this bug were wrong — “autoscaling drift”, “template value changed”, “it self-heals” — each plausible from whichever artefact I was looking at. On desiredCount questions, go to CloudTrail lookup-events EventName=UpdateService first; it is the only source that attributes the change.

2026-08-02 — Prompt #1424 [why is the magic-link email slow?]
it takes a long time to get a magic link email to login on Dev and stable. Why?

Answer: it is not SES. Measured both accounts — production access on, EnforcementStatus HEALTHY, Send == Delivery every day, zero bounces, zero rejects, and zero DELIVERY_DELAY events over 7 days on staging-b (the only env with a configuration set attached, so the only one with visibility). At 5-minute granularity Send and Delivery sit in the same bucket, worst case one bucket apart. SES hands off first attempt. The request endpoint is 6.2s cold / 0.6s warm.

Two real defects found underneath. (1) logging.basicConfig(level=...) is a silent no-op under Lambda because the runtime installs a root handler before user code imports — so LOG_LEVEL was ignored in all 15 FastAPI+Mangum services. Proven, not assumed: zero [INFO] and zero [WARNING] lines over 7 days on both auth functions while [ERROR] came through, and two probe requests that provably reached a logger.warning produced no record. Net effect: logger.info("Magic-link email send ... accepted=...") had never once been written — no server-side record of magic-link delivery existed at all. (2) The token TTL was 300s, shorter than real mail latency, so links were routinely expired on arrival → request another → wait again.

Remaining suspect for the residual delay is downstream of AWS: @3pp.com → @3pp.com same-domain mail into HostMonster shared107 inbound scanning.

Five items, ordered by payoff: (1) delete the bad 3pp.com apex MX — HostMonster DNS, Bill only; (2) measure the last hop by sending one link to Gmail and one to @3pp.com and comparing — the only unmeasured segment, and it tells you whether (3) is even the problem; (3) move the sender off @3pp.com — biggest lever, but reverses Bill’s 2026-07-03 directive; (4) add an SES configuration set to dev, which is currently blind to bounces and delivery delays; (5) ask HostMonster why inbound mail queues.

2026-08-03 — Prompt #1436 [send a test magic link and time it — DIAGNOSIS CLOSED]
send me a test magic link and time it → go, both tiers, [email redacted] and my gmail

Confirmed first that this needed approval — it sends real mail to a human inbox, always-confirm regardless of mode — and argued for a Gmail control arm, because a 3pp-only send gives a number with no baseline to interpret it against.

The experiment. Four requests fired in parallel within 13 ms, dev and staging-b × {3pp.com, a personal Gmail}. Same sender, same SES account, same instant; the only variable was the receiving infrastructure. All four logged accepted=True, zero unknown/inactive — a log line that had never once been written before this week’s fix.

SES was clean on both tiers: 4/4 Delivery events in the send minute, zero DeliveryDelay, zero bounces, zero rejects. SES records Delivery only on a 250 OK, and DeliveryDelay on any retry — so HostMonster accepted every message first-attempt within a minute and never deferred. Greylisting definitively ruled out.

Result: Gmail instant, 3pp.com minutes later. The entire delay is therefore after SMTP acceptance — inbound scanning or mailbox queueing on shared107. No AWS-side change can reach it.

Honest accounting: the TTL 300→900s change was the fix that mattered; the sender move did NOT improve arrival time and is not claimed to — it stays a net gain for DMARC alignment only. Said so plainly rather than letting the week read as a win.

Deliverable: docs/support/HostMonster_Inbound_Delay_Ticket .md + branded .docx, built with the existing generator (it already took SRC/OUT args). Render-verified, which caught two layout bugs invisible in the source — a collapsed metadata header and a list numbered 4–7 because Word continued numbering from an earlier list.

2026-08-03 — Prompt #1446 [CORRECTION — the HostMonster conclusion was overstated]
here is the header … → correct the three records, and the message was not a slow one

Bill supplied full headers. Decoded: DKIM t=1785805438 → sent 01:03:58 UTC; Received esmtps → shared107 accepted 01:04:40 UTC (+42s transit); Received LMTP → mailbox and Delivery-Date the same second. HostMonster’s internal queue time was zero. X-Spam-Flag: NO, score −0.7, Delivered-To ⇒ inbox, not Junk, not marginal.

That contradicts the conclusion I logged hours earlier (“the delay is inside HostMonster, after acceptance”). The A/B test proved where the delay is not — not SES, not transit, not greylisting — and left one region unmeasured: past SMTP acceptance. That region contains both HostMonster’s queue and the recipient’s mail client. I named the first when the evidence could not separate them.

Bill confirmed the sampled message was NOT a slow one, so I did not over-correct either: a fast sample cannot refute the slow path. Net position: mechanism unknown; established facts unchanged (SES clean, 0 DeliveryDelay, Gmail instant vs 3pp slow, custom MAIL FROM + new sender live in production per Return-Path: …@noreply.inspiresgenius.com and DKIM d=inspiresgenius.com).

Corrected three records: change_log (correction entry prepended + original heading marked SUPERSEDED IN PART, no content deleted), the memory, and the ticket — now banner-marked DRAFT / DO NOT SEND, claims restated to stop asserting a cause. Had it been sent as written, support would have produced this header and closed the case. Resolved and dropped: Inbox vs Junk.
